This could make way for an interview, or maybe an incident where SCP-02 is caught knowing information possessed by personnel whose mouths were taken.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This seems too random to really create a good atmosphere to me. SCPs should be bizarre, but they still need to remain consistant, with some sort of logic behind them, even if it's a twisted one.

Here, it seems like most of the elements only exist for the sake of convenience rather than to add to the SCP's identity: the tape isn't dangerous on its own so it gets a mysterious owner. But what if the owner dies? Better make him immortal. But if he's immortal, he can't be stopped and contained… welp, he's blind in bright lights now. But still, I'd like him to be a containment hasard so random power over electric locks and lights

Stuff like this doesn't make you think "how mysterious! I wonder what's the story behind this" but rather "well that just doesn't make any sense".

It doesn't grab the reader's attention, doesn't make them want to speculate, because there's nothing to really hold on to.

Frankly, I would do away with 933-02 entirely. I think it'd be a lot creepier if it were just the tape on its own, because then it makes you wonder where it comes from, who built it and why, etc… it feels a lot more uncanny to me when it's just a strange, possibly destructive object. Besides, at this point you have to wonder… how many victims did it take for the FOundation to notice the object? And who would have used it?

As they say, sometimes less is more.

SCP-933-02 has no facial features and doesn't need to breathe; since victims who have lost all their facial features are supposed to pretty much be SCP-933-02 except for not being superhuman, I assumed that they don't need to breathe, either.

What I'd like to know is, why does SCP-933-02 do what it does to people? Is it just to make everyone faceless for no particular reason other than that it can, or is it actually trying to achieve some sort of purpose? Maybe it's actually a slave to SCP-933-01, and SCP-933-01 is a sentient object that feeds on facial features somehow? I mean, Things What Eat You are overdone, but it would work here.

Also, Slender Man. :P

Upvoted because weird humanoid thing + seemingly regular thing that mutilates you. I mean, imagine losing your eyes, ears, nose, and mouth…That's four of the five senses gone right there… *shudder*

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: Might masking tape be more thematically appropriate? Aside from the unfortunate comedic association you've already mentioned, duct tape is for sticking things together whereas masking tape is for temporarily covering things up. Masking tape is associated with painting (change of appearance) and the word "masking" in its name is related to this object's effects.

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded:
An attached medical report is a good idea. An autopsy report, with the coroner getting progressively more and more freaked out by the distortions, would be better, IMO.

I suggested the tracheotomy kit because it's creepy. If you're reading this SCP for the first time, and you see that the Special Containment Procedures have the following sentence, sitting by itself:

"An emergency tracheotomy kit must be kept in the medical unit adjacent to SCP-933's enclosure at all times."

You start to wonder why. And then when you read about what 933 does in the Description section, the implications hit home, and you get that sinking feeling in your guts. At least, I do.

As for the other stuff, it's true that the Foundation's primary objective is S-C-P-ing, but they aren't just throwing personnel away, either. A faceless staffer is useful for things that work around eyesight or communication, as the interview with Agent whoever suggests. And an emergency tracheotomy isn't a complicated operation. You just make a small incision in the trachea and jam in a tube, then seal it shut. The condition of the jaw and nose don't actually matter for the procedure to work.

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded: You have to remember that the Foundation's top priority is to secure and contain these things, not to save everyone. Also, I said in the article that the feature is filled in with flesh and bone. Maybe I should include a medical report being more detailed, but in the case of the mouth, the jawbone is fused with the rest of the skull with no evidence of the teeth (or the rest of the mouth) ever being there. It would take considerable work to make someone able to function. Call me an amoral bastard, but it might be better to just let them die.
